Q: Validate Index for a Collection A:

I have a hard time to really understand your underlying requirement. As you know, you can access an entry of a collection either via index or via key. The index is an (long) integer, the key is a string (and always as string).

Using the index can be used to iterate over the collection. There might be cases where you know that a specific entry is on a specific index (e.g. you know that the main sheet of an Excel workbook is on index 1, but already that might fail). What you for sure never will have is the requirement to access an element by index and have a Double holding that index. If you have a situation like that, you have a design flaw. If, in any situation, you want to calculate the index of an entry from an floating number (eg "use index 1 for values between 0 and 1), the calling code must do this calculation, not any library function.

Using keys means that the calling code needs to know the key. If you have a date as key, the calling code needs to convert it into a unique string (maybe by using the Format-function), both when creating entry and when retrieving it. Don't implement such logic into a library function - you never know if the user needs an entry per day, per month, per hour...

(As you maybe already noticed, accessing an entry via key is magnitude faster than by index)

So your code should accept only (long) integer values and strings, everything else is an error. Don't do any magic conversations or let VBA do any implicit conversations for you.

Check the VarType of the variable. Assume that you are dealing with an index only if you have a vbInteger or a vbLong data type. Assume that you are dealing with an key only if you have a vbString data type. Throw an error (or whatever is needed in your case) for any other data type as they are not valid.

Some remarks to the edge case you have listed:

Platform: Dealing with integers as index and strings as keys is for sure compatible between operating systems. And as mentioned, all others point to a basic design flaw.

Numeric text: Is a string and not a number, so is will be uses as key, not as index. Quick prove:

Dim c As New Collection
c.Add "First element", "2"
c.Add "Second element", "1"
Debug.Print c(1), c("1")

prints

First element Second element

Numeric interpretation: There is no such thing as to interpret anything. A number is a number, a string is a string.

Numeric conversion: No need to convert anything. Especially the conversion from Empty to 0 you mentioned makes absolutely no sense.

Scientific notation: No such thing. Notation is a way to represent a number (on the screen or a printout or a text file). A Long (or Double) stores a number in an internal binary format, no matter if you display it as 1000 or 1e4. However, the string "1000" is something completely different as the string "1e4", and both are different from the numeric value 1000.

Rounding: Again, don't use any other numerical data type except integers as index, especially not if it holds fractions. If you need an entry for 3.14, convert it to a string and use it as key, not as an index.

Dates: The fact that dates are stored as Doubles internally doesn't qualify then as index. Side note: If you would use the day part (CLng(now)) as index, you first needs to make sure that for every date since 1.1.1900 an entry in your collection would exist. If you really want to access entries by date, convert them into a string explicitly, but that means you have a key, not an index.

Overlarge numbers: Firstly, this is not a real world problem - except if you have a collection with more than 2 billion entries. Anyhow, just to let you know, the following code will work:

Dim d As Double, c as New collection
d = 2147483647# * 2
If d > c.Count Then Debug.Print "Not in list"

Booleans: The fact that they are represented in VB* as integers doesn't qualify them as index.

Default members: An object doesn't qualify neither as index nor as key. That is also true for Uninitialized objects (Nothing).

If you are dealing with any data type that isn't an integer or a string, throw an error. Don't go down the rabbit hole "I don't want to bother the user with errors and therefore do all possible conversions silently" - it will just lead to errors that are hard to find.

Update: I think you misinterpreted my intension when saying "doesn't qualify". I didn't ment to say that it is technically not possible - it is simply that using anything other than an explicit integer or string is useless.

It simply makes no sence to pass an object, an empty variant, a date, a boolean or a double variable as index. And if you do so, you can almost be sure that the program contains a bug. Not throwing an error will hide that bug and either you or the user of your library will waste a lot of time to find it. Therefore it is much better to throw an error (your library should do this), even if the VBA collection would accept it. To be precise, it will not accept it, but the internal mechanism of VBA will implicitly try to convert the value into a number or a string, and implicit conversions are always bad, IMHO.

The fact that a Range variable is accepted as parameter is misleading. In fact it is not accepted. As the collection doesn't accept an object, VBA will use the default property which is it Value property. If the range variable contains only one single cell, this value might work as valid index (depending on the content of the cell).

Q: Git Bare repository fail. Missing necessary objects. Can't commit/push A:

I had normal dir and file backup of git repository in zip archive, which I used to restore, fix error.

  1. ~/git rename to ~/git_old_corrupted
  2. unzip git folders and files structured backup into ~/git
  3. commit and push to remote repository (one which was earlier corrupted)

This commit have pushed my all earlier commits at once.

Now it is back to normal again.

Q: Firebase signInWithRedirect() returns to my app, but never creates a Firebase Authentication user, while signInWithPopup() works A:

Based on how the redirect flow actually works under the hood: the real account-creation call (the accounts:signInWithIdp request to Identity Platform) happens on the /__/auth/handler page hosted at your authDomain, not in your app's own code. Since that call never results in a user, the most likely culprits are one of the following, roughly in order of probability given "everything else is identical":

  1. Browser storage partitioning / third-party storage blocking on the authDomain. If you're using the default *.firebaseapp.com authDomain rather than a custom domain, modern Chrome and Safari increasingly restrict that domain's ability to use IndexedDB/cookies from a hidden iframe when it's "third-party" relative to your app's origin. This breaks the state-matching Firebase relies on to complete the redirect round trip, and can prevent the handler page from finishing the exchange at all. The fix that reliably resolves this is switching your authDomain to a subdomain of your own app's domain (Firebase Hosting supports this) so it's treated as first-party storage.

  2. A request on the handler page is being silently blocked — by an ad blocker, privacy extension, or corporate/network filter blocking calls to identitytoolkit.googleapis.com or accounts.google.com. Since the handler page is a separate navigation, extensions that don't interfere with your popup (which stays on your origin) can still block resources loaded on the handler's page. Worth checking the Network tab specifically while the /__/auth/handler page is briefly visible, or testing in a clean profile with no extensions.

  3. Firebase App Check enforcement on Authentication. If App Check enforcement is turned on for the Auth product, the handler page's server call needs a valid App Check token; if that's missing/invalid during the redirect exchange, the sign-in gets silently rejected — same symptoms (visually completes, but no user, no result). Worth checking Firebase console → App Check → Authentication API to see if enforcement is on.

  4. Less likely but worth a quick check: calling signInWithRedirect more than once due to Angular change detection re-invoking the handler, or explicitly setting a non-default persistence (inMemoryPersistence/browserSessionPersistence) which can break the redirect flow since it depends on durable storage surviving the full page navigation.

I'd suggest starting with #1 (custom authDomain) since it's the most common cause of "popup works, redirect silently fails with no user created" reports right now, then checking the Network/Console tab during the handler page's brief appearance for blocked requests, then checking App Check settings.

Q: Install a personal firefox web extension permanently A:

It's 2025 and a lot of these answers are obsolete. According to this official documentation, these are your options:

Without a Mozilla account

Standard Firefox versions do not allow unsigned add-ons. However, there are special versions of Firefox that offer more flexibility:

  • Firefox Extended Support Release (ESR): Some versions allowed overrides, but most recent ESR releases also enforce signing.
  • Firefox Developer Edition and Nightly: You can disable signing checks here for testing.
  • Unbranded Firefox builds: These versions allow disabling signature enforcement, but they are primarily intended for developers and organizations.

To change the signature enforcement preference in supported builds:

  1. In the address bar, type about:config and press Enter.
  2. Click Accept the Risk and Continue.
  3. Search for:
    • xpinstall.signatures.required (extensions)
    • extensions.langpacks.signatures.required (language packs)
  4. Toggle the setting to False.

...

[If you want to install an add-on on Standard Firefox:] All add-ons must be submitted for signing, even if you distribute them outside addons.mozilla.org (AMO).

In other words, you'll have to use a different browser to permanently install unsigned extensions.

With a Mozilla account

This section is outside the scope of the question, but most people will probably be interested in it since it's by far the path of least resistance.

  1. Create a Mozilla Add-On account
  2. Upload your extension without publishing it on the official addon site
  3. Wait for it to be approved (sometimes this is automatic)
  4. Download it off the site (it'll be signed)
  5. Install it locally

This explanation is of little hand-wavy, but this official documentation goes into detail and includes useful images. Here's a way back machine link as a backup.
